source.name: Haute-Savoie surveyors, survey of 17 Sept 2026 (published 14 Oct 2026)

cross_check.name: Wikidata Q583 (P2044, CC0)

items.notes: The summit ice cap changes height: 4,810.02 m (2013), 4,807.81 m (2021), 4,805.59 m (2023), and 4,807.47 m in the survey of 17 Sept 2026 (published 14 Oct 2026, Euronews) — used here; Wikidata still holds the 2023 value (cross_check). SOVEREIGNTY: 'Ownership of the summit area has long been disputed between France and Italy' (Wikipedia); the border line near the summit and Dôme du Goûter is contested. Counted as the high point of both countries. Image: French (Chamonix) side.

items.subtitle: Sarawat Mountains

cross_check.name: Wikipedia: List of elevation extremes by country

items.notes: BOUNDARY: #50. Next is Iraq (Cheekha Dar, 3,611 m, #51), 55 m lower, so the boundary does not depend on any disputed value. Older sources quote 3,760 m for this peak; either value keeps it inside the top 50. Greenland (3,694 m) is not sovereign and is excluded. Image: distant view of the summit ridge from the Haraz (the photo Wikipedia uses).

insights.text: Mount Cameroon is often listed at 4,095 m, but satellite data puts it nearer 4,040 m.
Next: Mont Blanc. France and Italy still disagree over who owns its summit.
Next: Elbrus, Europe's highest peak, 835 m taller than Mont Blanc.
From here on, every peak tops 6,950 m, and 9 of the last 10 are in Asia.
India also claims K2. We list each peak under the country that controls it.

scope_note: What counts: the highest point of each sovereign country, listed under the country that controls it (de-facto administration). Summits on a border count for every country that shares them, so Everest appears for both China and Nepal and Mont Blanc for both France and Italy. Equal heights share a rank.
